Chapter 1: The Problem and Its Background
Background of the Study
       Creating music has always been a highly human activity. It comes from emotion, real life
experiences, and creative goals  [1]. However, Artificial Intelligence is rapidly changing how
people create and listen to music [2]. Modern computer programs can scan millions of songs to
learn complex patterns in rhythm and style. Because of this, they can generate new music
incredibly fast  [3]. Systems continue to push the realism of synthetic music through deep
generative architectures [4] and specialized language models [5]. Tools like Suno and Udio
show exactly how powerful  this technology  is today, using advanced networks to create
complete songs with vocals, lyrics, and instruments across many genres [6]. As these systems
become faster and produce higher audio quality [7], experts predict a massive shift in the music
industry. Artificial Intelligence will serve as a helpful assistant for casual creators. However, fully
automated generation threatens to flood platforms with synthetic songs. In the future, verified
human authenticity will become a highly valued premium commodity.

      The results of this shift are urgent and are already causing global backlash. A large
international survey by Deezer and Ipsos found that 97 percent of participants could not tell the
difference between human made and fully AI generated music [8]. Because people cannot hear
the difference, synthetic tracks are flooding streaming platforms. This directly threatens the
income of real musicians. Experts project a 12.7 billion dollar loss for musicians by 2028 [9],
alongside a massive drop in revenue [10]. In response, international artists are becoming
fiercely protective. The Artist Rights Alliance, which represents over 200 massive global artists,
recently released an open letter. They condemned the predatory use of Artificial Intelligence that
devalues human creativity [11]. Without reliable detection technology, the music industry cannot
protect authentic human work or ensure fair pay for artists.

       Existing  detection  tools  try  to solve  this problem, but they are technically weak.
Traditional machine learning methods provide a basic start [12], while newer networks try to find
visual and timing errors in the audio [13], [14]. Despite these efforts, international detection
systems fail in three major ways. First, the most advanced single mix models, like the Deezer
Autoencoder, achieve 99.8 percent accuracy in a controlled lab [15]. However, they completely
fail when the audio pitch is slightly shifted. They only look for software glitches instead of real
human musicality. Second, models like SpecTTTra ignore human biological vocal features. They
ignore natural breathing pauses and vibrato, which are proven signs of an authentic human
singer [16]. Third, systems that use two branches often process the entire blended audio file
without separating the vocals and instruments first. This creates messy data analysis. Finally,
these models fail heavily when tested on unseen AI platforms [17].

      The urgency of this problem goes beyond the global industry. It is acutely felt in the
Philippines. The Intellectual Property Office of the Philippines currently does not register AI
generated content for copyright [18]. This leaves human artists with very little legal protection.
National artist sentiments reveal deep frustration. Recently, the OPM community sounded the
alarm when an anonymous AI generated artist topped the Spotify Philippines Viral charts [19].
Filipino musicians argue that unregulated software monetizes local culture without permission

      To solve this, the researchers propose Know Ta. This is a Two Branch Deep Learning
Framework  for Cross Platform AI Generated Music Detection.  It also features Bayesian
Uncertainty Estimation. The main goal of this system is to accurately detect synthetic music by
analyzing the instruments and the voice independently. It does this by first separating the audio
layers using the Demucs source separation model [22]. Then,  it independently analyzes the
instruments through an EfficientNet B0 Audio Branch [23]. At the same time,  it analyzes the
biological vocal traits through a Bidirectional LSTM Vocal Branch [24]. The two branches are
merged using an attention mechanism that dynamically decides which branch is more important
for that specific song [25].

      Most importantly, the system aims to prevent falsely accusing a human artist. It uses
Monte Carlo Dropout [26] and Temperature Scaling [27] to produce a calibrated Bayesian
Confidence Score. This allows the system to provide exact percentage probabilities of how sure
it is about its decision. The system also features advanced conflict analytics. If the Audio Branch
detects AI but the Vocal Branch detects a real human, the system provides a specific
percentage analysis. It then notifies the user about the conflicting results. Finally, the system is
deployed as a simple web application. This allows anyone to access forensic level music
authentication without needing coding skills.

each song into instrumental and vocal stems. Each stem is analyzed in its own branch, and the
results are combined with attention-based fusion. The system also reports how certain  it is,
using Bayesian uncertainty.

Significance of the Study

      The authenticity of music has become an urgent concern in the digital era. With the rapid
creation of computer generated songs, human artists face unfair competition and loss of income
[9],  [10]. By combining stem separation [22], spectral audio analysis [23], biological vocal
tracking [16], [24], attention based fusion [25], and uncertainty estimation [26], this research
provides a complete and transparent solution. The findings of this study offer direct benefits to
several key groups across society, the music industry, and technology research.

Filipino Artists, the OPM Community, and Local Policymakers

       This study directly responds to the growing outcry among Filipino musicians, including
prominent P pop groups like SB19 [21] and traditional OPM artists [19]. Current copyright laws
under the Intellectual Property Office of the Philippines do not fully protect artists from having
their vocal styles copied by Artificial Intelligence [18]. Know Ta gives local creators a reliable
way to check whether their original work or vocal style has been replicated without permission.
For artists in regional cultural centers like Davao City, who often work independently without
expensive legal teams or major record labels, this tool helps protect their streaming royalties
and creative reputation [20]. Furthermore, it provides local policymakers with real technical data
on how synthetic music behaves, helping them create  fair and updated rules for creative
industries.

Independent Artists and Everyday Music Listeners

       Professional audio forensic tools are usually very expensive, highly technical, and locked
behind private studio software. Know Ta removes this barrier by packaging an advanced
detection model into a simple, free web application. Independent musicians can quickly upload
a suspicious song to see  if their work was stolen, while everyday listeners can check whether
their favorite songs were created by real people  [8]. Because the website outputs simple
percentage scores rather than confusing code, anyone can understand the results without
needing a technical background.

Computer Science and Deep Learning Researchers

       For researchers in artificial intelligence and audio forensics, this study provides practical
proof that separating audio into different layers produces better detection results than scanning

the broader field of synthetic media forensics.

Scope and Delimitation

       This study focuses on the design, development, and evaluation of Know Ta, a two
branch deep learning system created to  identify AI generated music tracks and provide

Scope of the Study

       generalization  is tested using the AIME dataset, which contains music from twelve
        different generation engines that the system never encountered during training [29]. Both
       datasets consist exclusively of ethical, non copyrighted, or Creative Commons audio,
       ensuring strict legal compliance.

       fusion layer then calculates learned weights to balance the importance of both branches

Delimitations of the Study

      To keep the research manageable within available resources, the study sets the
following limits:

    1.​ Language and Audio Style Limits: The system is trained and tested only on English
      language songs because the benchmark datasets are primarily recorded in English [28],
        [29]. The system does not evaluate songs in Filipino, regional Philippine languages, or
       other  foreign languages. Furthermore,  while the system handles songs with long
       instrumental solos,  it is not designed to evaluate purely instrumental genres, such as
        classical orchestra tracks, that have zero vocal content throughout the entire song.
    2.​ Model Selection Limits: The study chooses EfficientNet B0 for audio analysis and
        Bidirectional LSTM for vocal analysis based on prior benchmark performance [23], [24].
            It does not train or build other heavy computer vision backbones, such as ResNet, VGG,
       or Vision Transformers, beyond using them as comparison numbers from existing
         literature. For uncertainty estimation, the study does not implement Deep Ensembles
        [31], because  training  multiple independent models  requires too much computing
     memory and would make the simple web application too slow for everyday users.
    3.​ Operational and Legal Limits: The system functions purely as an analytical detector
      and does not include legal enforcement features, copyright takedown mechanisms, or
       watermarking capabilities.  It operates strictly on recorded audio files uploaded by the
       user in MP3 or WAV format and does not monitor live streaming audio feeds in real time.
        Finally, the project  is delimited to a desktop web browser interface; mobile phone
       applications and direct integrations with commercial streaming platforms like Spotify or
      Apple Music are left for future development.

Third, they leave out key design elements. A comprehensive benchmark found that detectors
work on blended audio without separating vocals from instruments, and that they ignore human
vocal biomarkers such as breathing pauses and vibrato [16]. The same benchmark named
multimodal detection as the most urgent open direction. Know Ta is built to answer this call.

Source Separation

     Demucs separates vocals and instruments from a mixed track directly in the waveform
domain [22]. Know Ta uses it so that each branch receives a clean input instead of a blended
one.

Spectral Analysis and the Audio Branch

        EfficientNet scales network width, depth, and resolution together, which gives strong
accuracy with far fewer parameters than older models [23]. In an audio deepfake benchmark on
Mel Spectrograms, EfficientNet B0 outperformed the other architectures tested [Bajwa et al.].
Mel Spectrograms themselves work better than MFCCs and chromagrams as input for CNN
audio classification [Wolf Monheim]. Together, these findings support the Audio Branch design
of Know Ta.

Vocal Analysis and the Vocal Branch

      Cues like vibrato and breathing pauses can only be identified with context from both
before and after a moment in the audio, which bidirectional networks provide [24]. In audio
deepfake tests, Bi LSTM beat both LSTM and Transformer models, reaching the best Equal
Error Rate (0.43 percent) and the highest accuracy [Al Hussaini et al.]. Adding prosodic features
such as pitch, timing, and glottal parameters to parallel LSTM modules also improves the
separation of real and fake audio [Muruganandham et al.]. The absence of regular breathing
and vibrato is a reliable, peer reviewed sign of machine generated audio [16]. These findings
support the Vocal Branch design of Know Ta.

modality never lowers expected performance [Huang et al.], so combining two branches can
only match or improve on either one alone. In practice, an attention based mixture of experts
ranked first overall in a major audio deepfake detection challenge [Negroni et al.].

stronger estimates but cost much more computing power [31], so they are left for future work.

Cross-Platform AI-Generated Music Detection with Bayesian

Uncertainty Estimation

A Computer Science Research Title Proposal

In Partial Fulfillment of the Requirements for Computer Science Research Methods

Delgado, Kent Paulo R. Delgado, Earl Josh B. Labay, John Renan N.

March 8, 2026

[Page 2]
Chapter 1: The Problem and Its Background Background of the Study Creating music has always been a highly human activity. It comes from emotion, real life experiences, and creative goals [1]. However, Artificial Intelligence is rapidly changing how people create and listen to music [2]. Modern computer programs can scan millions of songs to learn complex patterns in rhythm and style. Because of this, they can generate new music incredibly fast [3]. Systems continue to push the realism of synthetic music through deep generative architectures [4] and specialized language models [5]. Tools like Suno and Udio show exactly how powerful this technology is today, using advanced networks to create complete songs with vocals, lyrics, and instruments across many genres [6]. As these systems become faster and produce higher audio quality [7], experts predict a massive shift in the music industry. Artificial Intelligence will serve as a helpful assistant for casual creators. However, fully automated generation threatens to flood platforms with synthetic songs. In the future, verified human authenticity will become a highly valued premium commodity.

The results of this shift are urgent and are already causing global backlash. A large international survey by Deezer and Ipsos found that 97 percent of participants could not tell the difference between human made and fully AI generated music [8]. Because people cannot hear the difference, synthetic tracks are flooding streaming platforms. This directly threatens the income of real musicians. Experts project a 12.7 billion dollar loss for musicians by 2028 [9], alongside a massive drop in revenue [10]. In response, international artists are becoming fiercely protective. The Artist Rights Alliance, which represents over 200 massive global artists, recently released an open letter. They condemned the predatory use of Artificial Intelligence that devalues human creativity [11]. Without reliable detection technology, the music industry cannot protect authentic human work or ensure fair pay for artists.

Existing detection tools try to solve this problem, but they are technically weak. Traditional machine learning methods provide a basic start [12], while newer networks try to find visual and timing errors in the audio [13], [14]. Despite these efforts, international detection systems fail in three major ways. First, the most advanced single mix models, like the Deezer Autoencoder, achieve 99.8 percent accuracy in a controlled lab [15]. However, they completely fail when the audio pitch is slightly shifted. They only look for software glitches instead of real human musicality. Second, models like SpecTTTra ignore human biological vocal features. They ignore natural breathing pauses and vibrato, which are proven signs of an authentic human singer [16]. Third, systems that use two branches often process the entire blended audio file without separating the vocals and instruments first. This creates messy data analysis. Finally, these models fail heavily when tested on unseen AI platforms [17].

The urgency of this problem goes beyond the global industry. It is acutely felt in the Philippines. The Intellectual Property Office of the Philippines currently does not register AI generated content for copyright [18]. This leaves human artists with very little legal protection. National artist sentiments reveal deep frustration. Recently, the OPM community sounded the alarm when an anonymous AI generated artist topped the Spotify Philippines Viral charts [19]. Filipino musicians argue that unregulated software monetizes local culture without permission

[Page 3]
and drastically lowers the streaming payouts for real artists [20]. Also, Pablo, the leader of the internationally famous P pop group SB19, publicly condemned the unethical use of Artificial Intelligence. He stated that scraping an artist's identity and creative output without their consent should be completely illegal [21].

At the local level, Davao City reflects these national challenges. Independent and emerging local artists operate without the protection of a strong regulatory framework. The fear of being replaced by computer generated music is strong among local creators who lack the financial backing of major record labels. The absence of simple and accessible detection tools means that local artists and policymakers cannot verify authenticity. They lack the tools needed to protect homegrown musical works.

To solve this, the researchers propose Know Ta. This is a Two Branch Deep Learning Framework for Cross Platform AI Generated Music Detection. It also features Bayesian Uncertainty Estimation. The main goal of this system is to accurately detect synthetic music by analyzing the instruments and the voice independently. It does this by first separating the audio layers using the Demucs source separation model [22]. Then, it independently analyzes the instruments through an EfficientNet B0 Audio Branch [23]. At the same time, it analyzes the biological vocal traits through a Bidirectional LSTM Vocal Branch [24]. The two branches are merged using an attention mechanism that dynamically decides which branch is more important for that specific song [25].

Most importantly, the system aims to prevent falsely accusing a human artist. It uses Monte Carlo Dropout [26] and Temperature Scaling [27] to produce a calibrated Bayesian Confidence Score. This allows the system to provide exact percentage probabilities of how sure it is about its decision. The system also features advanced conflict analytics. If the Audio Branch detects AI but the Vocal Branch detects a real human, the system provides a specific percentage analysis. It then notifies the user about the conflicting results. Finally, the system is deployed as a simple web application. This allows anyone to access forensic level music authentication without needing coding skills.

Statement of the Problem This study develops and evaluates Know-Ta!, a two-branch deep learning framework that identifies human-made from AI-generated English-language music. It uses Demucs to split each song into instrumental and vocal stems. Each stem is analyzed in its own branch, and the results are combined with attention-based fusion. The system also reports how certain it is, using Bayesian uncertainty. ● How accurately does Know-Ta! classify songs as human-made or AI-generated, and how well does this hold on songs from AI generators it did not see during training? ● Does analyzing the Demucs-separated instrumental and vocal stems in two branches detect AI music better than analyzing the full mixed track as a single input? Does each branch also add value on its own? ● How well do the Bayesian uncertainty estimates match the model's actual correctness, so that the confidence percentage shown to users can be trusted, especially for ambiguous tracks?

● How reliably does the system's analytics detect and flag a conflict when the Audio Branch and the Vocal Branch disagree about whether a track is AI or human, and how clearly does it show which branch drove the result?

Significance of the Study

The authenticity of music has become an urgent concern in the digital era. With the rapid creation of computer generated songs, human artists face unfair competition and loss of income [9], [10]. By combining stem separation [22], spectral audio analysis [23], biological vocal tracking [16], [24], attention based fusion [25], and uncertainty estimation [26], this research provides a complete and transparent solution. The findings of this study offer direct benefits to several key groups across society, the music industry, and technology research.

Filipino Artists, the OPM Community, and Local Policymakers

This study directly responds to the growing outcry among Filipino musicians, including prominent P pop groups like SB19 [21] and traditional OPM artists [19]. Current copyright laws under the Intellectual Property Office of the Philippines do not fully protect artists from having their vocal styles copied by Artificial Intelligence [18]. Know Ta gives local creators a reliable way to check whether their original work or vocal style has been replicated without permission. For artists in regional cultural centers like Davao City, who often work independently without expensive legal teams or major record labels, this tool helps protect their streaming royalties and creative reputation [20]. Furthermore, it provides local policymakers with real technical data on how synthetic music behaves, helping them create fair and updated rules for creative industries.

Independent Artists and Everyday Music Listeners

Professional audio forensic tools are usually very expensive, highly technical, and locked behind private studio software. Know Ta removes this barrier by packaging an advanced detection model into a simple, free web application. Independent musicians can quickly upload a suspicious song to see if their work was stolen, while everyday listeners can check whether their favorite songs were created by real people [8]. Because the website outputs simple percentage scores rather than confusing code, anyone can understand the results without needing a technical background.

Streaming Platforms and Content Moderators

Streaming services currently struggle to manage the thousands of synthetic tracks uploaded to their libraries every day [8]. Most existing security filters use a simple label that only says real or fake, which often makes mistakes on songs that mix real vocals with generated beats. Know Ta solves this by offering detailed conflict analytics and separate percentage scores for the music and the voice. If a track contains real human vocals layered over an AI generated instrumental track, content moderators receive an immediate notification explaining

[Page 5]
the conflict. This allows platform staff to make fair, evidence based decisions rather than wrongly banning innocent human musicians.

Computer Science and Deep Learning Researchers

For researchers in artificial intelligence and audio forensics, this study provides practical proof that separating audio into different layers produces better detection results than scanning a blended song. It also shows how to add Monte Carlo Dropout to an existing neural network without rebuilding the entire system from scratch [26]. By proving that an attention mechanism can dynamically balance instrumental and vocal features [25], this research establishes a clear technical blueprint that future scientists can adapt for other fields, such as detecting deepfake podcasts, speech clones, and video audio.

Future Researchers

This study serves as a foundational reference for future researchers who wish to explore two branch architectures, Bayesian uncertainty estimation, or cross platform generalization in the broader field of synthetic media forensics.

Scope and Delimitation

This study focuses on the design, development, and evaluation of Know Ta, a two branch deep learning system created to identify AI generated music tracks and provide transparent confidence percentages. To ensure the project remains practical, focused, and scientifically valid, specific boundaries have been established.

Scope of the Study

The scope of this research covers the following areas:

1. Target Audio and Datasets: The study evaluates English language music tracks that contain both singing and instrumental accompaniment. Model training and initial testing use the SONICS dataset, which includes thousands of real human songs and synthetic tracks created by popular tools such as Suno and Udio [28]. Cross platform generalization is tested using the AIME dataset, which contains music from twelve different generation engines that the system never encountered during training [29]. Both datasets consist exclusively of ethical, non copyrighted, or Creative Commons audio, ensuring strict legal compliance. 2. System Architecture: The detection pipeline uses a structured sequence of established algorithms. The Demucs model first splits the input song into an isolated vocal track and an instrumental track [22]. The instrumental track is converted into a Mel Spectrogram image and analyzed by an EfficientNet B0 network [23]. The isolated vocal track is processed by a Bidirectional LSTM network [24] to measure biological traits such as breathing pause patterns [16], pitch stability, and natural vibrato. An attention based fusion layer then calculates learned weights to balance the importance of both branches based on the specific content of the song [25].

[Page 6]
3. Uncertainty Estimation and Analytics: The system includes Bayesian uncertainty estimation using Monte Carlo Dropout [26] combined with Temperature Scaling [27]. This setup allows the model to run multiple testing passes on the same clip, turning the variation of the results into an honest percentage confidence score. It also powers a conflict flag feature that detects and explains disagreements between the vocal branch and the audio branch. 4. Evaluation and Final Product: System performance is measured using six standard metrics recommended by international benchmark protocols: Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1 Score, ROC AUC, and Cross Platform Performance Drop Percentage [30]. The final output is delivered as a working, user friendly web application where users can upload standard audio files and view clear authenticity reports.

Delimitations of the Study

To keep the research manageable within available resources, the study sets the following limits:

1. Language and Audio Style Limits: The system is trained and tested only on English language songs because the benchmark datasets are primarily recorded in English [28], [29]. The system does not evaluate songs in Filipino, regional Philippine languages, or other foreign languages. Furthermore, while the system handles songs with long instrumental solos, it is not designed to evaluate purely instrumental genres, such as classical orchestra tracks, that have zero vocal content throughout the entire song. 2. Model Selection Limits: The study chooses EfficientNet B0 for audio analysis and Bidirectional LSTM for vocal analysis based on prior benchmark performance [23], [24]. It does not train or build other heavy computer vision backbones, such as ResNet, VGG, or Vision Transformers, beyond using them as comparison numbers from existing literature. For uncertainty estimation, the study does not implement Deep Ensembles [31], because training multiple independent models requires too much computing memory and would make the simple web application too slow for everyday users. 3. Operational and Legal Limits: The system functions purely as an analytical detector and does not include legal enforcement features, copyright takedown mechanisms, or watermarking capabilities. It operates strictly on recorded audio files uploaded by the user in MP3 or WAV format and does not monitor live streaming audio feeds in real time. Finally, the project is delimited to a desktop web browser interface; mobile phone applications and direct integrations with commercial streaming platforms like Spotify or Apple Music are left for future development.

Chapter 2: Review of Related Literature and Studies Related Literature

This chapter reviews the literature behind Know Ta. It starts with the rise of AI generated music and its impact, then looks at existing detection methods and where they fall short. It ends

[Page 7]
with the components Know Ta is built on: source separation, spectral and vocal analysis, attention based fusion, and Bayesian uncertainty estimation.

The Rise of AI Generated Music

Music has long been seen as an expression of human emotion and lived experience [1]. AI is changing that. Today's systems learn rhythm, harmony, and style from large song collections and can produce new songs at scale [3]. These tools are also reshaping how independent artists work [2]. Generative models such as Variational Autoencoders, GANs, and Diffusion Models drive much of this progress [4], [5]. Suno and Udio can create full songs with vocals, lyrics, and instruments [6], while ChatMusician shows that a language model can write music from a text prompt [5]. Computational intelligence keeps widening the range of music tasks that can be automated [7].

Industry and Economic Impact

The effects are already measurable. In a Deezer and Ipsos study, 97 percent of listeners could not tell AI music from human music [8]. Musicians could lose an estimated 12.7 billion dollars by 2028 [9], and creator revenue is projected to fall by 27 percent in the same period [10]. These numbers show why reliable detection is needed.

Legal, Regulatory, and Local Context

In the Philippines, AI generated content cannot be registered for copyright [18]. This leaves artists and developers in a legal gray area. Filipino artists now compete with tracks that cost almost nothing to produce, and musical works made up only 7 percent of copyright certificates issued in 2024. The OPM community raised the alarm when an anonymous AI "artist" topped the Spotify Philippines Viral chart [19]. SB19's Pablo publicly condemned the unethical use of AI and said that taking an artist's identity and work without consent should be illegal [21]. In Davao City, no regulation yet addresses how AI music affects local creators.

Traditional and Early Deep Learning Detection

Early audio classification relied on traditional machine learning. Support Vector Machines were used for genre classification [12], and SVM and Random Forest classifiers remain an interpretable but limited first step in detection. Convolutional Neural Networks later made spectral feature extraction efficient [13], and Recurrent Neural Networks captured timing patterns in music [14]. Transformers with attention improved the modeling of long range musical structure.

Limitations of Current Detection Systems

Current detectors have three main weaknesses. First, they are fragile. One detector reached 99.8 percent accuracy in controlled tests but collapsed after simple changes such as pitch shifting or codec re encoding, labeling every track as real once platform artifacts were

[Page 8]
gone [15]. Second, they do not generalize. A detector trained on one AI platform performs poorly on platforms it has never seen, so every new generator weakens existing tools [17]. Third, they leave out key design elements. A comprehensive benchmark found that detectors work on blended audio without separating vocals from instruments, and that they ignore human vocal biomarkers such as breathing pauses and vibrato [16]. The same benchmark named multimodal detection as the most urgent open direction. Know Ta is built to answer this call.

Source Separation

Demucs separates vocals and instruments from a mixed track directly in the waveform domain [22]. Know Ta uses it so that each branch receives a clean input instead of a blended one.

Spectral Analysis and the Audio Branch

EfficientNet scales network width, depth, and resolution together, which gives strong accuracy with far fewer parameters than older models [23]. In an audio deepfake benchmark on Mel Spectrograms, EfficientNet B0 outperformed the other architectures tested [Bajwa et al.]. Mel Spectrograms themselves work better than MFCCs and chromagrams as input for CNN audio classification [Wolf Monheim]. Together, these findings support the Audio Branch design of Know Ta.

Vocal Analysis and the Vocal Branch

Cues like vibrato and breathing pauses can only be identified with context from both before and after a moment in the audio, which bidirectional networks provide [24]. In audio deepfake tests, Bi LSTM beat both LSTM and Transformer models, reaching the best Equal Error Rate (0.43 percent) and the highest accuracy [Al Hussaini et al.]. Adding prosodic features such as pitch, timing, and glottal parameters to parallel LSTM modules also improves the separation of real and fake audio [Muruganandham et al.]. The absence of regular breathing and vibrato is a reliable, peer reviewed sign of machine generated audio [16]. These findings support the Vocal Branch design of Know Ta.

Attention and Multimodal Fusion

Attention lets a model weigh each input by how useful it is for the song being analyzed [25]. Simple concatenation performs worse than attention based fusion because it cannot suppress irrelevant information [Ranipa et al.]. Theory also shows that adding a complementary modality never lowers expected performance [Huang et al.], so combining two branches can only match or improve on either one alone. In practice, an attention based mixture of experts ranked first overall in a major audio deepfake detection challenge [Negroni et al.].

Ablation Methodology

[Page 9]
A component's contribution can only be claimed by removing it and measuring the change in performance [Meyes et al.]. Recent CNN Bi LSTM deepfake studies follow this same structure [Yadav and Mangalampalli; Murty et al.]. Know Ta adopts it for its six model ablation study.

Bayesian Uncertainty Estimation

Keeping dropout active during inference and running many forward passes approximates Bayesian inference, a technique called Monte Carlo Dropout [26]. This allows two kinds of uncertainty to be told apart: aleatoric uncertainty, which comes from ambiguity in the input, and epistemic uncertainty, which comes from gaps in what the model has seen [Kendall and Gal]. Know Ta adopts this distinction. Raw confidence scores are often poorly calibrated, and Temperature Scaling is a lightweight way to fix this after training [27]. Deep Ensembles give stronger estimates but cost much more computing power [31], so they are left for future work.

Evaluation Metrics and Benchmark Datasets

Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1 Score each capture a different side of performance and work best together [Sujon et al.]. Reporting only one metric is a known flaw in past detection research, and standardized multi metric evaluation is recommended [Chandra et al.]. ROC AUC adds a threshold independent way to compare systems [Jugade et al.]. For data, SONICS offers 97,164 English language tracks used for training and internal testing [28]. AIME provides AI platforms that do not overlap with SONICS, and is used only to test cross platform generalization [29].

Synthesis

The literature points to a clear picture. AI music is now hard to tell apart from human music [8], it threatens musicians' income [9], [10], and it is poorly regulated worldwide and in the Philippines [18]. Detectors, meanwhile, break under simple audio changes [15], fail on unseen AI platforms [17], and ignore both vocal and instrumental separation and human vocal biomarkers [16]. Each component Know Ta uses has already been validated in a related area: Demucs for separation [22], EfficientNet B0 for spectral analysis [23], Bi LSTM for vocal analysis [24], attention for fusion [25], and Monte Carlo Dropout for uncertainty [26]. No reviewed study combines them for cross platform, dual signal AI music detection. Know Ta fills that gap.

Theoretical Framework

Three theories support the design of Know Ta.

Bayesian Approximation Theory

A neural network with dropout kept active at inference, sampled over many forward passes, approximates a Bayesian posterior over its predictions [26]. Uncertainty can then be split into aleatoric (unavoidable ambiguity in the data) and epistemic (reducible uncertainty from

[Page 10]
limited model exposure) [Kendall and Gal]. This is why Know Ta uses Monte Carlo Dropout: it gives calibrated confidence scores instead of a single fixed prediction, which reduces the risk of overconfident false accusations against human artists.

Attention Theory

A model can learn to give different inputs different weights depending on their content, instead of treating all inputs equally [25]. This is the basis of Know Ta's fusion layer, which learns how much to trust the Audio Branch and the Vocal Branch for each track.

Multimodal Learning Theory

Adding a complementary modality never reduces expected utility [Huang et al.]. For Know Ta, this means that combining the Audio Branch and Vocal Branch, which capture different parts of a song, can only maintain or improve detection compared with either branch alone, as long as the fusion is well designed. This is the reason for the dual branch architecture.

Conceptual Framework

Based on these theories, Know Ta treats detection as a three stage pipeline of Input, Process, and Output, shown in the methodological framework in Chapter 3 (Figure 1).

● Input: English language audio tracks, both human made and AI generated, from the SONICS [28] and AIME [29] datasets. ● Process: Demucs separates each track into vocals and instruments [22]. Mel Spectrogram features go to the EfficientNet B0 Audio Branch [23], and prosodic features go to the Bi LSTM Vocal Branch [24]. An attention layer fuses the two outputs [25], and Monte Carlo Dropout produces Bayesian confidence estimates [26]. ● Output: A final label (Real or AI Generated), an overall Bayesian Confidence Score, separate confidence scores for each branch, a conflict flag when the branches disagree, and a real time authenticity report in the web application.
